meanings.def: (before a verb, as in 一...就...) as soon as; once

compositionNote: The simplest possible mark — one unbroken line — pictographically stands for the number one itself.
poem: One flat line upon the ground,
the very first count ever found.
No bend, no curve, just plain and true,
ONE (yī) is the stroke where numbers grew.

compositionNote: Simply two parallel lines stacked one above the other, doubling the single stroke of 一 to picture 'two'.
poem: Two flat lines, stacked up neat,
doubling one to make a pair complete.
Sky on top, the ground below,
TWO (èr) is how the counting starts to grow.

compositionNote: One more line stacked on 二 gives three parallel strokes, simply counting one higher.
poem: Add one more line atop the two,
now three flat strokes come into view.
Heaven, man, and earth in a row,
THREE (sān) is the trio, steady and slow.

compositionNote: A pair of legs (儿) fenced inside a boundary (囗) replaced the four tally-lines of oracle-bone script to write the number four.
poem: Legs tucked inside a fenced-in square,
a boxed-in strider, penned in there.
Four tally lines once stood in a row,
FOUR (sì) is the count this fence will show.

components.meaning: an X shape crossing between two bars, symbolizing interacting forces

compositionNote: An ancient X-shape crossing between two horizontal lines pictured heaven and earth's forces meeting, later fixed as the numeral five.
poem: Two flat bars with an X locked tight,
crossing forces of dark and light.
Where heaven and earth cross and bend,
FIVE (wǔ) is the count where they extend.

compositionNote: A small roof (亠) over two splitting legs (八) once pictured a simple hut; the shape was later borrowed purely for its sound to write six.
poem: A tiny roof with legs that splay,
a little hut from far away.
Borrowed now for sound alone,
SIX (liù) is the number that hut has grown.

components.meaning: a line crossed by a hooked cutting stroke

compositionNote: A horizontal line crossed by a hooked stroke once pictured cutting something in two; the shape was later borrowed to write the number seven.
poem: A line sliced through by a hooking blade,
an ancient cut that time has made.
Borrowed sound, forgetting the knife,
SEVEN (qī) counts through daily life.

components.meaning: two strokes curving apart, from a picture of something splitting in two

compositionNote: Two small strokes leaning away from each other originally pictured something being split apart; the shape was borrowed to write the number eight.
poem: Two little strokes that lean and part,
splitting cleanly right from the start.
Back to back, they gently sway,
EIGHT (bā) is the number that split away.

components.meaning: a bent, hooked arm, from an ancient pictograph

compositionNote: A single curling stroke once pictured a bent elbow or hooked arm; borrowed for its sound, it became the numeral nine.
poem: A curling hook, an elbow bent,
an ancient arm's own shape it lent.
Twist and turn, then curve some more,
NINE (jiǔ) sits one shy of a perfect score.

components.meaning: a vertical line crossed by a horizontal one, from a knot tied in a tally cord

compositionNote: A simple cross shape once marked a knot tied in a counting cord for every ten items, giving the character its meaning of ten.
poem: A cross of lines, both straight and true,
a knot once tied when counts hit ten.
Vertical meets horizontal too,
TEN (shí) is the round count born again.

meanings.def: fragmentary; odd; leftover (as in extra small amounts)

compositionNote: Rain (雨) falling as scattered drops gave the original sense of 'fragment, remainder', while 令 lends the sound líng; the word later came to mean 'zero', the emptiest fragment of all.
poem: Raindrops scatter, fragment, fall,
tiny remnants, that is all.
An order (令) gives the sound so clear,
ZERO (líng) is the emptiest drop of the year.

compositionNote: One (一) capping 白, which lends its sound (bái becoming bǎi), builds the numeral for a full hundred.
poem: One small stroke sits on top of white,
a hundred units, gleaming bright.
White (白) lends its sound, plain to hear,
A HUNDRED (bǎi) counted, loud and clear.

meanings.def: generic measure word for people or objects

components.meaning: a single stalk of bamboo, from an ancient pictograph

compositionNote: The character began as a picture of one stalk of bamboo standing among many in a grove, making it a natural generic counter for individual things.
poem: One lone bamboo stalk stands tall,
a single stem among them all.
Count the stalks one by one, you see,
EACH (gè) item gets its own bamboo key.

components.meaning: a person walking, seen from the side

compositionNote: A simple pictograph of two legs in mid-stride, viewed from the side, drawing a person in motion.
poem: Two legs striding, side in view,
one leg forward, walking through.
A simple sketch of you and me,
PERSON (rén) is all humanity.

components.meaning: an ancient serrated halberd or weapon

compositionNote: The character originally drew a jagged, saw-toothed weapon; because its sound matched, it was borrowed to write the first-person pronoun 'I', losing its weapon meaning entirely.
poem: A jagged blade with saw-tooth bite,
an ancient weapon, sharp in sight.
Its shape stuck, but not its blow,
'I' (wǒ) is all it means, you know.

compositionNote: A person (亻) stands beside 尔, an old word for 'you' that also lends its sound, pointing straight at the person you're speaking to.
poem: A person standing right by 尔,
the ancient word that once meant 'you'.
Point a finger, greet them well,
YOU (nǐ) is the one I'm talking to.

compositionNote: A person (亻) next to 也, which supplies the sound tā, forms the third-person pronoun 'he'.
poem: A person leans on 也 too,
also here, as people do.
Not you, not me, but someone new,
HE (tā) is the other person in view.

compositionNote: A woman (女) paired with the sound-giving 也 (tā) created the modern feminine pronoun 'she', coined in the early 1900s to mirror 他.
poem: A woman stands by 也 as well,
also here, the same to tell.
Swap the person for the girl,
SHE (tā) steps into the word-whirl.

compositionNote: The character began as a picture of a coiled snake tucked beneath a roof-like curve; it later lost that literal meaning and was borrowed as the pronoun 'it'.
poem: A snake once curled beneath its roof,
tail tucked in, safe and aloof.
No longer slithering, just a name,
IT (tā) is what non-humans became.

meanings.def: plural marker attached after pronouns or people

compositionNote: A person (亻) beside a door (门), which lends its sound men, marks that more than one person is passing through — the plural suffix.
poem: One by one through the door they come,
person after person, not just one.
The gate (门) lets many pass again,
PLURAL is marked by this little men (men).

components.meaning: a bird flying upward, disappearing from sight

compositionNote: The character originally pictured a bird flying up until it vanished from view — the idea of something no longer being there gave rise to the negative 'not'.
poem: A bird flies up and out of sight,
vanishing into fading light.
Gone from view, it won't come back,
NOT (bù) is what that bird will lack.

compositionNote: The sun (日) sits above a mark for 'straight, correct' (正, shown in a slightly altered form), the idea being that what the sun reveals is true — hence 'to be; is'.
poem: The sun shines straight and never lies,
correct and true beneath the skies.
What the sun sees, it will affirm,
'TO BE' (shì) is the sun's own certain term.

meanings.def: possessive/attributive particle linking a modifier to a noun ('s, of)

compositionNote: The character originally pictured something bright and clear (白) marked by a small ladle-shaped stroke (勺), meaning a clear 'target'; this common word was later borrowed as the everyday possessive particle 'de'.
poem: Bright white target, clear and small,
a tiny ladle scoops it all.
Just a little linking key,
POSSESSIVE de ties things, you see.

meanings.def: marks a completed action after a verb
marks a change of state at the end of a sentence

components.meaning: a bent hook, from an ancient picture of a swaddled child

compositionNote: The character once pictured a swaddled child with arms wrapped close to the body; the sense of being 'bound up, finished' led to its use as the marker of completed action.
poem: A tiny hook, all bent and small,
a swaddled babe, arms wrapped and all.
Wrapped up snug, the deed is done,
COMPLETE is le — the action's won.

meanings.def: to be located at; to exist
(before a verb) in the process of

compositionNote: Standing firmly on the earth (土), with 才 lending its sound zài, the character expresses being located somewhere.
poem: Feet planted firm upon the earth (土),
rooted right where you find your worth.
Talent (才) whispers its sound today,
LOCATED here is where you stay (zài).

compositionNote: A hand (又, shown as the slanted stroke on top) reaching down to grasp a piece of meat (月, originally 肉) pictures the basic act of possessing something.
poem: A hand reaches down, grabs some meat,
holding tight to something to eat.
Grip it firm, don't let it go,
TO HAVE (yǒu) is the oldest 'possess', you know.

compositionNote: Movement (辶) paired with a sound-component (文, simplified from the original phonetic 言) points to something close at hand as you move toward it — 'this'.
poem: Walking (辶) toward the words (文) you see,
step by step, right up close to me.
Point right here, no need to guess,
THIS (zhè) is the one within your reach.

compositionNote: A phonetic element from an ancient place name (冄) stands beside the 'city' radical (阝, from 邑), since 那 first named a distant region before it came to mean 'that'.
poem: A far-off town (阝) with a name of old,
a place (冄) whose story has been told.
Point across the distant plain,
THAT (nà) is the far one, not so plain.

compositionNote: A mouth (口) asking a question sits beside 那 (nà), which supplies the sound, turning 'that' into the question word 'which'.
poem: A mouth (口) pops open, asking 'that'? (那)
Which one, though? Point me where it's at!
A curious voice with a questioning air,
WHICH (nǎ) one is it — tell me where.

compositionNote: Spoken words (讠) beside a little bird (隹, lending its sound zhuī toward shéi) form the question word asking about an unnamed person — 'who'.
poem: Words (讠) fly out to ask about a face,
a little bird (隹) sings from its place.
A mystery voice calls through the air,
WHO (shéi) is singing? Tell me who's there.

compositionNote: A person (亻) next to the numeral ten (十) originally named a squad of ten soldiers; today the character survives mainly in the question word 什么, 'what'.
poem: Ten (十) soldiers standing in a line,
one person (亻) counted every time.
Now the meaning's shifted, though —
WHAT (shén) could this old squad still show?

meanings.def: toneless suffix with no meaning of its own, used in 什么, 这么, 那么, 怎么

components.meaning: a thin twisted thread, from a picture of fine silk (a variant of 幺)

compositionNote: The character pictures a small twisted strand of silk — something tiny and slight — and today survives only as a light, toneless suffix in words like 什么 and 怎么.
poem: A tiny thread, so thin and light,
twisted silk, barely in sight.
No weight of meaning does it hold,
just a soft SUFFIX (me), story untold.

meanings.def: turns a statement into a yes/no question

compositionNote: A mouth (口) asking something sits beside 马 (mǎ), which lends its sound, forming the simple question particle 'ma' placed at the end of a sentence.
poem: A mouth (口) pops open to ask, you see,
a horse (马) gallops by, wild and free.
Tack it on the end of what you say,
QUESTION particle ma — yes or nay?

meanings.def: softens a question or asks 'and...what about...?'

compositionNote: A mouth (口) speaking sits beside 尼 (ní), which lends its sound, forming the soft question particle 'ne' used to ask 'and what about...?'.
poem: A mouth (口) leans in, soft words it lends,
a gentle nun (尼) whose calm tone bends.
'And what about...?' the question flows free,
that lingering NE (ne) finishes gently.

compositionNote: Grain (禾, also lending its sound hé) feeding a mouth (口) pictures shared food and contentment, giving the sense of 'harmony', which extended to the everyday connector 'and'.
poem: Grain (禾) shared out to feed each mouth (口),
peace grows in from north to south.
Link one thing with another, see —
AND (hé) joins us all in harmony.

compositionNote: Walking (彳) alongside 艮, a stubborn, unyielding element that lends its sound gěn toward hěn, intensified over time into the everyday adverb 'very'.
poem: Steps (彳) march on, stubborn and set,
hard as stone (艮), no doubt or fret.
Push it further, to the max degree —
VERY (hěn) means 'to the utmost', you see.
